One of the coolest things we did, while in the rainforest, was interact with the K'iche' people who live there.

Their society is much different than ours. What we might consider trash, they often use to make things like wallets (wallets out of milk cartons, for instance) or jewelery (earrings, pendants). There is often no electricty and people live in simple huts. Most are slightly elevated because of the rainfall.

The K'iche' children get to school via canoe, and there is no medical care for miles around. At one point, there had been a hospital boat built to float along the river, but it was built to incorrect specifications and continually got caught in the muck. The nearest hospital was about 5 hours away by flight, and it was an hour canoe ride to get to the nearest city with an airport.

With that in mind, the K'iche' have created their own ways of healing, and have employed shamans to help.

Our guide introduced us to one such shaman. An old man, living in a hut surrounded by a huge garden - it had much of what he would need to sustain himself with.

Our guide spoke to him, and lead us onto the old man's porch. We weren't a large group, just a few. It was almost surreal.

The shaman did not speak English and most of us did not speak Spanish. So we sat, and waited for our guide to translate for us.

In the end, the shaman blessed us using leaves, tobacco and smoke. We were told to close our eyes and he chanted and hit us with the leaves, then blew smoke in our faces.

For all I know, he could've been telling us to screw off, but it was pretty neat. [Here's a photo of some of us being blessed](http://imgur.com/BDDn0Lg).
[Amazon Rainforest, Ecuador] Getting Blessed by a K'iche' Shaman
I wonder how the K'iche' people see us, and how strange they must find our ways. I hope they get a better hospital though, modern medicine can really help tribes like this.

They like Americans because we give them money when we visit their villages (Ecuador runs on the US dollar). Or at least they pretend to like us. The thing I came away with from them, is that if they can be happy with next to nothing, what excuse do I have? They also know all about the forest and what plants can cure what. There's a dragonblood tree that has sap that stops bleeding for instance. The guide we were with knew how to use it.

Knowing what sap can coagulate blood can be truly life-saving for those people, it makes perfect sense they'd have great knowledge of it. I'm sure they like American tourists because their economy is somewhat dependent on the tourism, and that's better than their land being cut down for "progress".

That is a huge issue for them. Our guide grew up in the forest and told us how a lot of the land is being bought by oil companies, and how people feel very forced into signing contracts because their neighbors who they share land with want money from it, but it's absolutely destroying parts of the forest. And relationships, of course.

A lot of people are so poor in that country. The minimum wage is 300 USD a month, so around 210 pounds. I have no idea how people live off of that. In the forest it is harder too, but they have natural resources that they use. They fish and grow food very efficiently. We got to eat the food that they eat, and it's really good.
